How the in-service code itself divides the work: inspector and examiner

Direct answer: API 510 does not leave the Level II versus inspector question to custom. It names two roles. The examiner performs specific NDE and does not evaluate the results under the code unless the owner/user has trained and authorized them to. The inspector evaluates and accepts all NDE results. The examiner needs method competence, not API certification; the inspector needs API certification, not method certification.

The definitions are worth reading in your licensed copy of the current API 510 edition (the eleventh edition of October 2022, with errata), because they settle most arguments on site. In our own words, API 510 says the following about the examiner role:

  • The examiner supports the inspector by carrying out specified NDE on vessel components.
  • Evaluating those results against API 510 is not part of the examiner role unless the owner/user has specifically trained and authorized the person to do it.
  • An examiner is not required to hold API 510 certification and is not required to be an employee of the owner/user.
  • The examiner must be trained and competent in the NDE procedures being used, and the owner/user may ask for certifications as proof. API 510 gives ASNT SNT-TC-1A, ANSI/ASNT CP-189 and AWS welding inspector certification as examples.
  • The inspector's employer keeps the examiners' certification records, and those records must be available to the inspector.

On the inspector side, API 510 makes the inspector answerable to the owner/user for making sure inspection, NDE and pressure testing meet the code, expects the inspector to be directly involved in the field, and allows the inspector to be assisted by examiners and operating personnel, while keeping evaluation and acceptance of all NDE results with the inspector. API 570 and API 653 use the same structure for piping and tanks. That is the code-level reason a Level II's report is an input, and the inspector's evaluation is the decision.

Two consequences follow for owners. First, an owner can legitimately staff a vessel inspection with a contractor's NDT examiners and its own (or a contracted) API 510 inspector; nothing in the code requires the same company, or the same person, to do both. Second, the owner decides what proof of examiner competence it requires. "SNT-TC-1A Level II in UT under the contractor's written practice" is a common answer; "ASNT central Level II" or "CP-189" are others; in Canada it is usually NRCan certification to CAN/CGSB-48.9712.

One vessel, two roles: walking through an on-stream inspection

Direct answer: On a typical on-stream vessel inspection the inspector plans the work and decides afterwards; the Level II examiners produce the measurements in between. The hand-off point is the NDE report. Following one job end to end shows where each credential's authority starts and stops.

Before the job. The owner's API 510 inspector reviews the inspection plan for a carbon steel separator: the credible damage mechanisms for that service, the condition monitoring locations (CMLs), the previous thickness data and corrosion rates, and whether an on-stream inspection may substitute for an internal one under the code's conditions. The inspector specifies what NDE is needed and where: UT thickness at the CMLs, a scan of the bottom head and boot where water may collect, and a shear-wave or phased array examination of a nozzle weld flagged at the last turnaround.

During the job. The UT Level II checks the procedure, calibrates the instrument and probe on a reference block of suitable material and thickness, verifies calibration at the intervals the procedure requires, takes the readings and records them against CML identifiers. The PAUT examiner sets up the scan plan, confirms coverage, and records and sizes any indications to the procedure's rules. Neither examiner calculates remaining life or comments on fitness for service.

The report. The examiners' report lists equipment and serial numbers, calibration, procedure and revision, examiner name and certification level, readings, scan coverage, indications with location and size, and any limitations (for example, surface condition or access).

After the job. The API 510 inspector compares the new readings with history, calculates short-term and long-term corrosion rates, checks the minimum required thickness, calculates remaining life, and sets or confirms the next inspection date within the code's limits and the owner's quality system. If the nozzle weld indication needs more than the code's inspection rules can resolve, the inspector refers it to the owner's engineer for evaluation. If a repair is needed, the inspector authorizes and accepts the repair inspection under the code.

Every decision in the last paragraph rests on the quality of the data in the paragraph before it. That is why owners care just as much about the examiner's certification as the inspector's, even though only one of them signs for the equipment.

Advanced UT: where examiner qualification goes beyond Level II

Direct answer: For crack detection and sizing, a general UT Level II may not be enough. API 510 lets the owner/user call for industry-qualified UT shear wave examiners for certain flaw detection and sizing work, and API runs QUTE programs for manual UT, phased array UT and thickness measurement examiners. These are examiner qualifications, not inspector authority.

API's Individual Certification Programs list includes QUTE (Manual), QUTE (Phased Array) and QUTE-TM (thickness measurement). They test whether an examiner can detect and size flaws, or measure thickness, under performance-demonstration conditions. Owners typically specify them for higher-consequence work: sizing cracks in wet H2S service, monitoring known flaws between inspections, or examining welds where UT is substituting for radiography. A QUTE-qualified examiner is still an examiner under the code: the API 510 or 570 inspector evaluates the results.

From a career point of view, this is a third path that sits between "Level II" and "API inspector": method depth that is portable and recognized by owners. It pairs naturally with ASNT Level III in UT for people who want to own procedures. Where these overlap and differ is covered in our comparison of ASNT Level III and API QUTE ultrasonic scopes.

Regulatory overlay: OSHA PSM, state laws and Canadian provinces

Direct answer: Neither credential is a government license on its own. They gain force because regulations require inspection to follow recognized practice and be documented, and because some jurisdictions name their own inspector credentials. Check the jurisdiction before assuming either certificate is sufficient.

OSHA PSM. For covered processes, 29 CFR 1910.119(j)(4) requires inspection and testing to follow recognized and generally accepted good engineering practices (RAGAGEP), at frequencies consistent with manufacturers' recommendations and good engineering practice, and requires each inspection to be documented with the date, the name of the person who performed it, the equipment identifier, a description of the work and the results. Employers that adopt API 510, 570 and 653 as RAGAGEP inherit the codes' inspector/examiner split, and auditors will check that NDE was performed by qualified examiners and evaluated by the inspector. 1910.119(j)(3) separately requires training for employees involved in maintaining the ongoing integrity of process equipment.

State boiler and pressure vessel laws. Many states require jurisdictional inspection of certain pressure vessels by National Board commissioned inspectors, and some recognize owner-user inspection organizations. Whether an API 510 inspector satisfies the state requirement for a given vessel depends on the state law. Confirm with the state chief inspector's office.

Canada. NDT certification in Canada is generally through Natural Resources Canada, which certifies personnel to CAN/CGSB-48.9712 and states that the standard satisfies ISO 9712. SNT-TC-1A certification is seen on some projects, especially with US-based owners, but should not be assumed to be accepted. In-service pressure equipment inspection is regulated provincially. In Alberta, ABSA's AB-526 sets the requirements for the In-service Pressure Equipment Inspector certificate of competency, which applies to people who conduct or certify integrity assessments of in-service pressure equipment, and AB-506 sets inspection and servicing requirements for owner-user programs. Ontario regulates through TSSA. An API certificate may be valued by employers in Canada but does not replace a provincial requirement.

What API eligibility asks of an NDT technician

Direct answer: NDT field work can count toward API inspector eligibility, but API decides what counts. For API 510, 570 and 653, API's program pages list education and experience combinations, and every combination requires at least one year in supervision or performance of inspection activities as described in the relevant code.

API's published combinations run from one year of experience for a bachelor's degree or higher in engineering or technology, through two years for a two-year technical degree or certificate and three years for a high school diploma, up to five or more years for candidates with no formal education. API 570 additionally states that experience must have been gained within the last 10 years. Read the current program page before applying, because the tables are revised.

For a Level II, the practical question is whether the work you do is "inspection activities as described in" the code, or only examination. A UT technician who also reviews CML data, records condition, participates in inspection planning or supports the inspector's evaluation is building that experience; someone who only collects readings on instruction may have a harder time documenting it. Keep a log as you go: equipment, dates, activities, and a supervisor or inspector who can verify them.

The reverse also applies. An API-certified inspector who wants to perform NDE needs method certification under an employer's written practice (or a central program), with the training hours, experience hours, vision exam and practical exam that requires. Neither path shortcuts the other.

Common mistakes when comparing or combining the two

  • Treating Level II as "junior API". They are separate ladders. A UT Level III is not an API inspector, and an API 570 inspector is not a UT examiner unless separately certified.
  • Letting the examiner evaluate by default. Under API 510, evaluation against the code is not the examiner's role unless the owner/user has specifically trained and authorized it. If your program does authorize examiners to evaluate certain results, write it down.
  • Missing examiner records. The code expects examiner certification records to be maintained and available to the inspector. Ask for them before mobilization, not after a finding.
  • Specifying "Level II" without the method. A Level II in MT cannot perform the UT survey.
  • Using the wrong API program. API 510 covers vessels, 570 piping, 653 tanks. A tank evaluation signed by someone holding only API 510 may not meet the owner's program.
  • Ignoring the jurisdiction. State commissions and provincial certificates can be required for the same work.
  • Letting clocks drift. API's three-year cycle carries a work-activity requirement; method certifications renew on their own cycle. Track both.

Verifying both credentials before work starts

Direct answer: API certificates are verified centrally; NDT certifications under SNT-TC-1A are verified through the employer's records. Owner QA teams should check both before mobilization.

API offers a public Inspector Status Verification tool, searchable by last name or certification number, and an ICP directory searchable by program and, in the US and Canada, by state or province. For an SNT-TC-1A Level II, ask the contractor for its written practice and the individual's certification record: method and level, training and experience hours, examination results, vision exam date and the Level III who approved the certification. ASNT central certificates and NRCan certificates can be checked with the issuing body. A clean file for each examiner, plus a verified API status for the inspector, is what an auditor will look for when the PSM documentation trail is tested.

How Atlantis supports both sides

Atlantis NDT works on the examiner side of this split. Our technicians are ASNT-certified under ASNT Level III oversight and perform UT thickness and CML surveys, corrosion mapping, PAUT, TOFD, MT, PT and VT, with certification records available to owner QA. Results go to the owner's API-certified inspector, who stays inspector of record; we are not the authorized inspector or inspection agency. For technicians building the NDT side of a career, we deliver ASNT SNT-TC-1A training online, live-virtual or onsite, with 1,000+ technicians trained. We do not offer API certification training or exam prep. See NDT Level II training and ASNT certification paths, ask for a Level II training plan, or book ASNT-certified NDE examiners. We reply to quote requests within 24 hours.

More questions about Level II and code inspector roles

Does an NDT examiner need API 510 certification?

No. API 510 says examiners need not hold API 510 certification or be employed by the owner/user, but must be trained and competent in the NDE procedures used. The owner/user may require proof such as SNT-TC-1A or CP-189 certification.

Can a Level II evaluate results against API 510?

Only if the owner/user has specifically trained and authorized them to. Otherwise evaluation and acceptance of NDE results belong to the inspector.

Is ASNT Level II accepted in Canada?

Canadian NDT certification is usually through NRCan to CAN/CGSB-48.9712, which NRCan states satisfies ISO 9712. Some projects accept SNT-TC-1A; confirm with the owner. Provincial rules, such as ABSA's AB-526 in Alberta, govern who may certify in-service pressure equipment inspections.

Does PSM require API-certified inspectors?

OSHA's PSM standard does not name API certifications. It requires RAGAGEP-based inspection, documentation and training. Employers that adopt API 510, 570 and 653 as RAGAGEP follow the codes' inspector requirements.

What is QUTE and do I need it as a Level II?

API's QUTE programs qualify UT examiners for manual or phased array flaw detection and sizing, and QUTE-TM for thickness measurement. Owners specify them for certain scopes. They add to, rather than replace, employer certification.

Does NDT field experience count toward API 570?

It can, if it includes inspection activities as described in API 570. API requires at least one year of such activity in every eligibility route, with experience gained in the last 10 years. API decides what qualifies.
